item.title: Regional Analytics Consent for Static Sites with CloudFront and Terragrunt
item.description:
A static site can be built by GitHub Actions, uploaded to S3 and served through CloudFront without an application server. Adding Google Analytics is also easy: paste a tag into the page template. Deciding when that tag may load takes more care.

The decision can depend on a country, a US state and a visitor’s saved choice. The HTML is the same for everyone, but the analytics default should not always be the same. I implemented this on five static sites, including duns.me and scomp.me, using a small CloudFront endpoint. The pages stay static and share the same cache. The edge answers one dynamic question.

item.title: Six Years Without Reinstalling Fedora: When 65 GiB Free Wasn't Enough
item.description:
This Fedora installation has been upgraded in place since Fedora 33. The rescue initramfs on this ThinkPad is dated 26 December 2020, and the same installation is now running Fedora 44 with 7.2.x kernels in /boot. More importantly, its Btrfs filesystem was created at the same time and has never been reformatted.

Both / and /home are Btrfs subvolumes on the same 475.4 GiB nvme0n1p3 partition. The operating system, containers, caches, user data, and build trees therefore compete for one storage pool that carries nearly six years of allocation history.

item.title: scomp-agent: My tmux Sessions on the Phone, Without SSH and Without Open Ports
item.description:
I start long jobs in tmux. Then I go away from the laptop. Then I want to know if the job is finished. For many years, my procedure was this: find a laptop, connect a VPN, open SSH, attach to tmux, and read one line. That is five steps to read one line.

The phone is always in my pocket. The terminal session is always on a server. I wrote scomp to connect these two things. This post is about scomp-agent, the small Go binary that runs next to your sessions.
